lesson_title: The Chip Stall and the Hawkers
hook_text: A chip stall begging the rank committee for help just invented every trade barrier on earth.
clip_script: Inside the taxi rank, one chip stall has fed commuters for years. Then hawkers appear along the fence — vetkoek, boerie rolls, cheaper and often fresher. Takings halve. So the stall owner goes to the rank committee, and listen to her requests, because she is inventing the entire toolkit of protectionism. Charge every hawker thirty rand a day to trade at the fence — that's a tariff. License only four hawkers, names on a list — a quota, and watch those four suddenly love the rule, because the licence itself is now worth money. Give the stall free use of the cold room — a subsidy, invisible to commuters but real. Demand health certificates from the fence but not the stall — a standard, sincere or convenient. And her darkest suspicion: one hawker selling below cost on purpose, planning to raise prices once the stall dies — dumping, the one accusation even the hawkers' friends take seriously. Now count both sides like the committee must. Protect the stall: two workers keep jobs, rent keeps flowing — visible, grateful gains. But two thousand commuters pay about two rand more for lunch every single day — a loss so thin nobody marches, yet it adds up to more than the stall ever gains. That is protection's arithmetic everywhere: the rescued shop makes the news; the two thousand lighter pockets never do.
visual_style: A bustling illustrated taxi rank in bold flat colours: one glowing chip stall inside, a fence line of hawker umbrellas outside; each request stamps onto the screen as an official-looking rubber stamp — TARIFF, QUOTA, SUBSIDY, STANDARD, DUMPING.
mood: Wry and revealing, ending on a sober punch of arithmetic.
pacing: Rapid stamp-by-stamp beats through the five requests, then a slow, deliberate final count of the two sides.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to weigh protection against free trade — and climb the ladder from taxi rank to AfCFTA.
